content: gatewayd listens on port 8443 in staging and 9443 in production; its health probe is GET /healthz on the admin port 8444.
scanlink serves gRPC on port 7311 and exposes Prometheus metrics on port 7312.
manifestd binds port 8610; its readiness endpoint is /ready, not /healthz.
The retry cap for manifest uploads is set with MANIFESTD_RETRY_LIMIT (default 5).
scanlink reads SCANLINK_RETRY_LIMIT for handheld sync retries; the default is 3 and the maximum accepted value is 10.
Set ROUTEKIT_SOLVER_TIMEOUT_MS to cap how long the route solver may run for one request; the default is 1500.
Error code E4012 from gatewayd means the API key is valid but the tenant is suspended.
Error code E4021 from gatewayd means the request body failed schema validation; check the X-Manifest-Version header first.
Error code SL-209 from scanlink means the handheld clock skew exceeds 90 seconds.
manifestd returns MF_DUP_BARCODE when two parcels in one manifest share a barcode.
The nightly manifest reconciliation job is defined in deploy/cron/reconcile.yaml and runs at 02:15 UTC.
Start the local stack with `make dev-up`; `make dev-down` also removes volumes, so use `make dev-stop` to keep your data.
The flag --dry-run-routes on `tern-cli plan` prints the computed routes without writing them to the database.
`tern-cli plan --max-stops 40` limits the number of stops per route; the default is 25.
Ticket PW-1042 tracks the duplicate-barcode bug in manifest import; it was fixed in release 2.14.1.
Ticket PW-1024 is the request to add pagination to the /v2/parcels endpoint; it is still open.
The staging S3 bucket for scanner firmware is tern-fw-staging-eu; production uses tern-fw-prod-eu.
SQL migrations live in db/migrations and carry a four-digit prefix, for example 0087_add_depot_index.sql.
The local dev Postgres connection string is read from PARCELWISE_DB_URL; the test suite uses PARCELWISE_TEST_DB_URL.
Feature flags are defined in config/flags.toml; the flag route_cache_v2 gates the new route matrix cache.
The label printing queue is named labels:print:v1 and its dead-letter queue is labels:print:dlq.
beacon sends SMS through the provider named in BEACON_SMS_PROVIDER; the allowed values are gateway-a and gateway-b.
ledgerbox generates invoices on the 3rd of each month with the job invoice_monthly in ledgerbox/jobs/invoice.py.
The load-test script is scripts/loadtest/spike.js; run it with `k6 run -e TARGET=staging scripts/loadtest/spike.js`.
The Grafana dashboard UID for solver latency is rk-solver-latency.
The on-call rotation changes at 09:00 Monday Europe/Berlin; the pager alias is tern-primary.
The depot import CSV must be UTF-8 without a BOM, with columns in the order depot_id, name, lat, lon, timezone.
The Docker base image for every Python service is registry.tern.example/base/py312:2026.10.
Lint with `ruff check services/` and type-check with `mypy --strict services/routekit`.
Integration tests need TERN_IT_ENABLED=1 in the environment; without it they are skipped silently.
JWT signing keys rotate every 30 days; tokens carry the key id in the kid header and gatewayd publishes keys at /.well-known/jwks.json.
Scanner firmware versions are written fw-<major>.<minor>.<patch>-<channel>, for example fw-4.2.0-beta.
Never run `make dev-down` with the shared staging cluster as your kubectl context; it drops the manifestd volume. Check `kubectl config current-context` first.
The routekit solver is not thread-safe: calling Solver.solve from a thread pool corrupts the cost matrix. Use one process per worker.
manifestd silently truncates barcodes longer than 48 characters; validate the length before import.
A SCANLINK_RETRY_LIMIT above 10 is ignored without any warning and falls back to the default of 3.
The staging database is reset every Sunday at 03:00 UTC, so any test data created there is lost.
Never point the k6 spike test at production; the gatewayd rate limiter trips and pages the on-call.
Timestamps inside manifests are local to the depot, not UTC; convert with the depot timezone column before comparing.
Do not hand-edit files under services/routekit/proto_gen; regenerate them with `make proto`.
Never renumber an applied migration in db/migrations; checksums are verified at startup and the service refuses to boot.
Port 8443 collides with the Docker Desktop Kubernetes dashboard on some laptops; set GATEWAYD_PORT to move gatewayd locally.
The label printer firmware drops jobs larger than 64 KB without raising an error; split big ZPL payloads.
The CI cache key includes the lockfile hash, so any change to poetry.lock throws away the 4 GB wheel cache and slows the next build by about ten minutes.
Route solver latency spikes were caused by unindexed depot lookups; adding idx_depot_region cut p95 from 2.1s to 340ms.
Flaky scanlink tests came from real clocks; freezing time with the fake_clock fixture removed the flakes.
Printing labels in batches of 50 beat per-parcel prints; the printer queue stopped backing up.
Most E4021 errors seen in staging came from clients still posting manifest schema v1 after the move to v3.
manifestd cold starts are dominated by loading the depot cache (about 8 seconds); keep at least two warm replicas.
A solver timeout paired with a greedy fallback gave the best on-time rate; exact solving only paid off beyond 60 stops.
Autovacuum lagged on the parcel_events table during bulk imports; lowering autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 fixed the bloat.
Handhelds on 2G looked offline because the heartbeat interval was 5 seconds; raising it to 20 seconds fixed the false offline state.
Property-based tests on the route cost function found a negative-weight edge case that example tests missed.
Invoice rounding drift came from summing rounded line items; sum integer cents and round once at the end.
Every service exposes /healthz for liveness only and /ready for dependency checks.
New endpoints follow handler, then service, then repository layering; handlers never import repository modules directly.
Background jobs are idempotent and keyed by job_key; retries reuse the same key.
Config is read once at startup into a frozen Settings dataclass; there are no os.environ reads in request paths.
Errors that cross a service boundary are wrapped as ServiceError(code, message, retryable).
Database tests use a per-test transaction rolled back at teardown, through the db_session fixture.
New features ship behind a flag in config/flags.toml first; removing the flag is its own PR within two releases.
Commit messages follow conventional commits and carry the ticket id, for example feat(routekit): cache matrices [PW-1187].
Use RabbitMQ as the broker for the label printing queue.
Label printing moved from RabbitMQ to Redis streams because ops no longer wanted to run a separate broker.
gatewayd authenticates tenants with static API keys only.
gatewayd moves to short-lived JWTs signed with rotating keys; static API keys stay only for legacy tenants until PW-1100 lands.
Static API keys are removed entirely as of release 2.16; the legacy tenants were migrated to JWTs.
Use OR-Tools CP-SAT as the primary route solver.
Replaced CP-SAT with a custom insertion heuristic plus local search because CP-SAT was too slow beyond 40 stops; CP-SAT is kept only for offline audits.
All services target Python 3.11.
The baseline is raised to Python 3.12 and 3.11 support is dropped, so every service shares one base image.
Use Alembic for schema migrations.
Schema changes are plain numbered SQL files run by a checksum runner; Alembic autogenerate produced diffs nobody could review.
Branch with GitFlow, using long-lived release branches.
Switched to trunk-based development with short-lived branches and release tags, because long-lived release branches caused merge drift.
Services log plain text lines through logging.basicConfig.
Services log structured JSON with structlog and put request_id on every line, so logs can be joined across services.
Keep parcel scan events for 365 days.
Scan event retention is cut to 180 days to meet the data-minimisation policy; older events are aggregated and the raw rows deleted.
Cache route matrices in process memory.
Route matrices are cached in Redis under the key prefix rk:matrix: so replicas share them; the change is behind the flag route_cache_v2.
CI runs on self-hosted Jenkins.
CI moved to GitHub Actions with hosted runners; Jenkins was decommissioned at the end of Q3 because nobody wanted to patch it.
beacon sends delivery notifications by SMS only.
Delivery notifications go out as push first and fall back to SMS after 10 minutes, because SMS was the largest beacon cost.
Handhelds sync by polling the REST API every 30 seconds.
Handhelds sync over a persistent gRPC stream to scanlink instead of polling, because polling drained batteries.
Version the public API with an X-Api-Version request header.
The public API is versioned in the URL path (/v2/...); header versioning confused caching proxies.
Tests run against SQLite for speed.
Tests run against a real Postgres container, because SQLite hid dialect bugs in the parcel_events queries.
Secrets live in .env files committed encrypted with sops.
Secrets are fetched from the vault at boot and the sops-encrypted .env files were deleted from the repo.
Each service lives in its own repository.
Services were merged into one monorepo called tern-platform so proto changes land atomically.
Money is stored as integer cents plus an ISO currency code, never as floats.
Depot ids are opaque strings; code must never parse meaning out of the prefix.
Parcel ids are ULIDs so that they sort by creation time.
gatewayd rate limits each tenant to 600 requests per minute with a token bucket.
Production deploys happen on Tuesdays and Thursdays only; there are no Friday deploys.
We support only the latest two scanner firmware majors; fw-3.x handhelds are end-of-life.
Code review needs one approval, and two for any change under services/ledgerbox.
Public API deprecations get six months notice and a Sunset response header.

2026-10-06 gatewayd rollout notes, taken from the PW-2231 incident review. Rollouts go canary, then 25%, then 100%, with a 12 minute soak between stages. The canary stage is started with `tern-cli rollout --service gatewayd --stage canary --soak 12m`. The load balancer sends 5% of tenant traffic to the canary pool, chosen by a hash of the tenant id, so one tenant always lands on the same pool for the whole rollout. Auto-abort fires when the 5xx ratio on the canary stays above 1.5% for two consecutive scrapes. While a pod drains, gatewayd waits for in-flight requests; the wait is capped by GATEWAYD_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_S (45 in production, 10 in staging), after which the remaining connections get a GOAWAY. The full checklist, including the manual rollback steps, is in ops/runbooks/gatewayd-rollout.md. Ignore the older ops/runbooks/gatewayd-rollout-v1.md, which still points at the Jenkins job that no longer exists. Second topic from the same review: the status page entry for a gatewayd incident is posted by the incident commander within 15 minutes using the template in ops/templates/status-update.md, and the customer-facing component name is Public API, never gatewayd. Third: the canary pool is the Kubernetes deployment gatewayd-canary with the label track=canary, and its autoscaler is capped at 4 replicas by maxReplicas in deploy/helm/gatewayd/values-prod.yaml, so a canary cannot absorb more than four pods' worth of traffic even when the 5% share is large.

scanlink shutdown behaviour, written down after the Harbor Depot night-shift complaint on 2026-09-29. A scanlink node that receives SIGTERM stops accepting new handheld streams immediately, tells connected handhelds to reconnect with a random jitter of 0-8 seconds, and then keeps serving the streams it already has. Handhelds are expected to be gone within the grace window set by SCANLINK_DRAIN_GRACE_S (30 seconds by default); anything still attached after that is cut off. To drain a single node by hand use `scanlink-ctl drain --node scan-07`, and check progress with `scanlink-ctl streams --node scan-07`. The Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds must always be larger than the drain grace plus 10 seconds, or the kubelet kills the pod mid-drain. This was tracked as PW-2240. Separate topic: the node names scan-01 to scan-12 are pets, not cattle, because of the sticky depot assignment, so do not scale in by deleting arbitrary pods. Unrelated but from the same notes: handheld pairing QR codes expire after 10 minutes, and the pairing endpoint is rate limited to 5 attempts per device per hour, which returns the error SL-452 on the sixth attempt; support can reset the counter with `scanlink-ctl pairing reset --serial HX2-004417`. We also agreed that depot supervisors, not engineers, own the decision to take a node out of rotation during a shift, and that the announcement template is ops/templates/node-drain-notice.md. Streams per node are exported as scanlink_streams_active, and the alert ScanlinkNodeImbalance fires when one node carries more than twice the average.

Incident digest for the week of 2026-10-12, manifestd section. Nothing else in the digest needed action: the certificate renewal was done early and the staging database was resized over the weekend. manifestd was OOM-killed three times in the week of 2026-10-12 while sealing the very large Northgate manifests. The immediate cause is that each upload batch is buffered in memory in full before it is validated, and batches over a few thousand parcels blow past the container limit of 2Gi. The log line to grep for is `MF_OOM_7 batch exceeds memory budget`; when you see it the pod is already on its way to being killed, because the check runs after the allocation. The batch size is governed by MANIFESTD_BATCH_BYTES (default 8388608, which is 8 MiB); do not raise it without also raising the memory limit in deploy/helm/manifestd/values-prod.yaml, where resources.limits.memory currently says 2Gi. Staging uses deploy/helm/manifestd/values-staging.yaml and has a 1Gi limit, so an upload that works in staging can still die in production. Follow-up ticket is PW-2262; the proper fix is streaming validation. In the same week we also found that the Northgate depot uploads manifests with trailing whitespace in barcodes, which manifestd trims silently; this is harmless but explains odd diffs in the audit log. The dashboard panel for memory per pod is called manifestd-memory and lives in ops/dashboards/manifestd.jsonnet.

Performance retro, scanlink, October. We keep a running list of latency investigations here so the next person does not repeat them; the earlier entries blamed the network, which was wrong. This entry is the one that actually found the cause. scanlink p99 sync latency doubled in early October and it took two days to find out why. The flame graph on 2026-10-09 showed 40% of the time inside the per-scan fsync in the write-ahead buffer; every incoming handheld scan was flushed on its own. The fix was to coalesce scans and flush on a timer: SCANLINK_BATCH_FLUSH_MS=250 brought p99 back from 1.9s to 420ms without losing durability for our purposes, because the handheld keeps its own queue until it is acknowledged. Things that did not help: more replicas, a faster disk class, and raising the gRPC window size. A caveat for the future: if the flush interval is raised above 500 ms the handheld acknowledgement timeout of 800 ms starts to fire and produces duplicate scans. The change was PW-2307. Also noted while there: the pprof listener is off by default in production and must be switched on per node.

scanlink config cheat sheet, kept up to date by whoever touches the Helm chart; written because three different people asked the same questions during the October release week and the answers were scattered over chat threads and two outdated wiki pages. Format: what it is, what it defaults to, where it is set. Verified against the chart on 2026-10-15 by reading the rendered manifests rather than the templates. scanlink batching and limits, as configured on 2026-10-15. Besides the time-based flush, scanlink also flushes when the buffered scans reach a byte threshold: SCANLINK_BATCH_FLUSH_BYTES (default 65536, i.e. 64 KiB). Whichever limit is hit first wins. The scanlink admin API, used by scanlink-ctl, is served on port 7410 and must never be exposed outside the cluster; the public gRPC port 7311 is a different thing. A single handheld upload that is larger than the hard cap of 4 MiB is rejected with error SL-317 (batch too large), and the handheld app is supposed to split it and retry. If you see SL-317 in the logs more than a handful of times per hour, a handheld build is probably not splitting uploads, which is a client bug rather than a server one. Values for each environment live in deploy/helm/scanlink/values-prod.yaml and deploy/helm/scanlink/values-staging.yaml. Operational reminder: the scanlink liveness probe is /healthz on a small HTTP listener and takes no dependency into account, whereas /ready checks the write-ahead buffer volume; during a disk-full event only /ready turns red, so a pod can be alive and not ready for a long time. Disk alarms on the buffer volume trigger at 80% under the alert name ScanlinkBufferDisk.

Debugging diary, handheld support, Harbor Depot, 2026-10-21. Morning: an operator at the Harbor Depot reported that three of the twelve handhelds on the night shift had stopped syncing after the shift handover and showed a red banner instead of the scan screen. Rebooting did not help for two of them. Support first suspected the Wi-Fi access point on the east wall, because the three devices had all been docked there, and spent about an hour on cable and signal checks; the access point logs were clean. Afternoon: engineering looked at the server logs and found the actual signal. What follows is what we learned. Handhelds reporting SL-371 are not misbehaving; SL-371 means the handheld session token has expired and the device must log in again. We spent a morning on 2026-10-21 chasing it as a clock problem because the sibling error SL-209 is the clock-skew one, and the numbers look alike. Typical cause: the device was docked overnight and the token lifetime of 12 hours elapsed. The fix on the server side is nothing; on the device, the operator re-scans the badge. Do not raise the token lifetime to hide the errors, because the security review (SEC-109) capped it at 12 hours. For debugging only, scanlink can expose pprof and expvar on port 7401, enabled with SCANLINK_DEBUG_LISTEN=1 on one node; remember to turn it off again and never port-forward it from production without telling the on-call. Note that 7401 and 7410 are easy to mix up: 7410 is the admin API, 7401 is the debug listener.

Design notes on partitioning, manifestd, from the architecture sync of 2026-10-02. We spent most of the hour on whether to move to a separate database per depot group and decided against it for now, because cross-depot reporting would then need a federation layer that nobody wants to own. The smaller outcome of the meeting, which is the part worth keeping, is below. manifestd shards parcels by depot so that one busy depot cannot slow down the rest. The shard for a manifest is computed as crc32(depot_id) % MANIFESTD_SHARD_COUNT, and the count is 16 in production and 4 in staging. Every table that holds per-parcel data carries a shard_key smallint column and is partitioned on it; new tables must do the same, and queries must always include shard_key in the WHERE clause or they will scan every partition. The column was introduced by services/manifestd/migrations/0047_add_shard_key.sql in September. Changing the shard count is not a config tweak: it needs a repartition job and a freeze on uploads, and the last time it was discussed (2026-10-02) we decided to over-provision at 16 so that we never have to. Reminder from the review: depot ids are opaque, so hashing them is fine but never derive the shard by looking at the id prefix. Side notes from the same thread: the partition naming scheme is parcels_p00 to parcels_p15, and the query that spots a skewed shard is `select shard_key, count(*) from parcels group by 1 order by 2 desc limit 3`. Shard 11 carries about 22% of the volume because of the Northgate depot, which is why the capacity alert ManifestdShardSkew uses a ratio and not an absolute number. The next review of the shard plan is due after the peak season, tracked in PW-2395, and until then nobody should propose a new shard key for anything.

Support FAQ draft for the manifest API, section on sealing. These were collected from the last two weeks of customer tickets so that the answers can go into the public documentation once reviewed; they have not been reviewed by the API owners yet, so treat the wording as internal. A pattern in the tickets: customers read the error codes as if they were HTTP statuses, which they are not, and several assumed that a retry is always safe, which is the root of the first item. Two entries are especially easy to confuse, so they are kept together. Two errors that look alike when sealing manifests. MF_SEAL_409 means the manifest was already sealed, usually because a client retried the seal call after a timeout; it is safe to treat as success if the seal token matches, and unsafe if it does not. The setting MANIFESTD_SHARD_SIZE is deprecated since 2026-09-18 and ignored by all versions after 3.8; do not set it, because the old documentation still mentions it and people keep adding it to Helm values. The migration that removed its column is services/manifestd/migrations/0074_drop_shard_size.sql (note the number: it is 0074, not 0047, which is the one that added the shard key). If a client sees MF_SEAL_409 with a fresh seal token, that is a real conflict: two clients are sealing the same manifest, which points to a duplicated depot-gate integration. Escalate to the manifestd owners with the manifest id.

Reference sheet for depot operations, manifestd, last updated 2026-10-18 after the DST follow-up. Depot managers asked for something they can read without opening the code, so this entry is deliberately written in plain terms and the technical names are in brackets. Items are in the order operators meet them during a normal evening. Manifest sealing has a daily cutoff. After the cutoff a depot can no longer seal manifests for that day, and the API answers with MF_SEAL_490 (sealed after cutoff). The cutoff is evaluated in the depot's own local time, defaults to 21:40, and is set in config/manifestd.toml under the key seal.cutoff_local; individual depots can override it in the depot_overrides table. The check uses the IANA zone stored on the depot, not the server's zone, which caused the DST incident PW-2266. Do not confuse MF_SEAL_490 with MF_SEAL_409, which is a double seal, nor with MF_DUP_BARCODE. A sealed manifest is immutable; late parcels go onto the next day's manifest. Ops can grant a one-off extension with `manifestd-ctl extend-cutoff --depot nrth-02 --minutes 30`, and every extension is written to the audit log with the requesting ticket.

Route matrices are cached in Redis for 15 minutes. ROUTEKIT_MATRIX_TTL_S=900 in every environment. The reasoning: traffic estimates from the map provider refresh every 10 minutes, and a matrix older than that gives drivers ETAs that are visibly wrong. Cache keys keep the existing rk:matrix: prefix and include the depot id and a hash of the stop set. Decided on 2026-08-11 by the routing team; the memory cost of the short TTL was accepted. Revisit if the map provider bill grows, because every cache miss is a paid matrix call. The matrix builder in routekit/matrix/builder.py calls the provider in chunks of 25 origins by 25 destinations; at roughly 900 stops per depot per day that is the main variable cost of routing, which is why the TTL is a knob we watch. Warm-up after a Redis flush takes about 6 minutes and is acceptable at the current volume. Owner is the routing team, reviewed monthly.

Route matrix TTL raised from 15 minutes to 1 hour: ROUTEKIT_MATRIX_TTL_S=3600 from release 2.19 onward. Reason, from the 2026-10-27 cost review: the map provider bill had grown by 38% and most matrices were requested again within the hour with the same stop set, so the 15 minute TTL was throwing away paid results. Accuracy was measured on a sample week; ETAs from the cached hour-old matrices were within 4% of fresh ones outside of rush hour. Rush hour (06:30-09:30 and 16:00-19:00 local) is handled by a separate shorter TTL, ROUTEKIT_MATRIX_TTL_RUSH_S=600, so the old behaviour is kept where it matters. Do not set the TTL in hours; the variable is in seconds. This replaces the earlier 900 second decision; ticket PW-2349.

Observability notes for the routing team, collected during the 2026-10-30 incident and tidied afterwards on 2026-11-03. During the incident people kept asking where to look, so this is the short list of what exists and what it means; the longer explanation of the solver itself is in the design document and is not repeated here. The incident was resolved in about two hours once the cause was found. routekit observability, as of 2026-11-03. The metric that counts how often the solver gave up and used the greedy fallback is routekit_solver_fallback_total, labelled by depot and reason (timeout, infeasible, memory). A healthy depot sits under 3% of requests; above 8% for ten minutes fires the alert ROUTEKIT-ALERT-14, whose runbook entry is OPS-518. The Grafana dashboard for it has the uid rk-solver-9f2 and lives in ops/dashboards/routekit-solver.jsonnet. A different alert, ROUTEKIT-ALERT-41, is about matrix cache misses and is documented under OPS-581, so check the numbers before pasting a ticket link. The solver timeout that triggers the timeout reason is ROUTEKIT_SOLVER_TIMEOUT_MS, which is in the facts already. During the 2026-10-30 incident the fallback rate hit 31% because a depot's stop list contained duplicate coordinates. Notes on the dashboard: the panel 'fallback by reason' is a stacked graph, and the 'matrix cache hit ratio' panel uses routekit_matrix_cache_hits_total divided by routekit_matrix_requests_total. The hit ratio target is 85% in the working day. After the TTL decision the ratio rose from 71% to 88%.

Geocoding clean-up week, notes by the data quality group. Short version: two jobs failed for different reasons and the team conflated them in standup, so the details are recorded here to keep the ticket numbers straight. Geocoding batch jobs kept failing on 2026-10-08 for two different reasons that looked identical. First, the nightly job sent 1,000 addresses per call and pinpoint rejected them; the working size is `pinpoint-cli geocode --batch-size 200`, and that fix was PW-2412. Second, a few hours later the same job failed with HTTP 429 from the upstream tile provider; that was the rate limiter and is a separate ticket, PW-2421, fixed by lowering concurrency and not by changing the batch size. When both numbers come up in a conversation, remember that 2412 is the batch size and 2421 is the rate limit, and the digits are swapped on purpose by nobody. Also learned: geocode results with confidence below 0.6 should be queued for manual review instead of being written to the depot table, and the review queue is the table geocode_review. A few other things from that week's geocoding clean-up. Addresses written in capitals geocode worse than mixed case, and the normaliser in pinpoint/normalise.py now title-cases the street name before the lookup; that alone raised the match rate from 91% to 94%. Postcodes are never edited. The review queue geocode_review is worked by the depot clerks, and an item that sits for more than 5 days is auto-resolved to the depot centre by the job geocode-expire, which was a deliberate compromise with operations. We also decided not to pay for the premium geocoding tier, because the clerks' manual fixes cost less than the subscription.

beacon notification templates live in services/beacon/templates/ as one MJML file per template, plus one JSON file per locale in services/beacon/templates/locales/. Rendering falls back from the recipient's locale to the language, and then to en. A template is not usable until it is listed in templates/index.toml, which is a common reason for a notification that silently never goes out. Push notifications are sent in batches: BEACON_PUSH_BATCH=500 messages per provider call, with one retry for the whole batch and then per-message retries. Subject lines and push titles are capped at 60 characters, and the linter in scripts/check_templates.py rejects longer ones. Template changes need a screenshot of the rendered email in the PR, which is the one rule that gets forgotten most. SMS is handled differently and has its own batch size.

beacon notification costs and delivery rules, summarised from the 2026-10-19 review with finance and the compliance team. The review covered push, email and SMS; email is cheap and unremarkable and is left out here. The consent angle matters more than the money, so the relevant provider behaviour is recorded in some detail below, with the codes people will meet in logs and support tickets. beacon SMS delivery goes through the provider textrelay (a stand-in name used in our docs). SMS is sent in batches of BEACON_SMS_BATCH=50, much smaller than the push batch, because textrelay throttles larger calls and bills rejected ones. Phone numbers are normalised to E.164 before sending. The provider answers BC-88 when the recipient has opted out of messages from our sender id; in that case the number is added to sms_optout and never retried, which is required by our consent policy. Do not mistake BC-88 for BC-808, which is the quiet-hours deferral. Delivery receipts arrive on a webhook and are matched to the notification by provider_message_id; unmatched receipts older than 24 hours are dropped by the sweeper. Cost note from 2026-10-19: one SMS costs about nine times a push, which is why push-first was chosen.

beacon behaviour that surprises people, recorded after the complaint from a recipient who got a delivery message at night in October. The short answer is that the system is supposed to be quiet at night, and the rest of the story is below. beacon does not send delivery notifications during recipient quiet hours, 21:00 to 07:00 in the recipient's local time. A message that would fall inside the window is not dropped: it is deferred and the attempt is recorded with status code BC-808. Enforcement is behind the flag beacon.quiet_hours.enforce, which is on in production since 2026-10-14 and off in staging, so test results differ between the two. Do not confuse BC-808 with BC-88, which means the recipient opted out and is permanent. Urgent categories (failed delivery attempt, parcel held at depot) bypass quiet hours only if the template sets urgent = true, and the compliance team reviews that list each quarter. The tracking ticket for the original complaint was OPS-581, not OPS-518; the latter is a routekit alert runbook. Time zones come from the address, and if there is none we use the depot zone.

Finance engineering handbook, ledgerbox section 4. This page is for engineers who touch the ledger code but are not accountants; the accounting terms are explained inline. It is based on the walkthrough Finance gave us on 2026-10-31 and on the runner code as of that date. Review it again whenever the close procedure changes, since the calendar belongs to Finance and not to us. ledgerbox month-end close, summarised on 2026-10-31. The close runs once per period at 03:00 UTC on the first day of the following month, configured with LEDGERBOX_CLOSE_HOUR_UTC=03. It is executed by services/ledgerbox/close/runner.py, which takes a period lock, posts accrual entries, runs the balance checks and then marks the period closed. To rehearse it, use `ledgerbox-ctl close --period 2026-10 --dry-run`; the dry run writes nothing and prints the entries it would post. Finance owns the calendar, and engineering must not move the hour without them. The close takes about 40 minutes for the full parcel volume, and the longest step is the tenant-by-tenant balance check. A close that is interrupted can be resumed and does not repeat entries, because every entry carries a deterministic entry_key built from the period and the tenant id. Other things engineers keep asking about the close: the accrual account codes are in services/ledgerbox/close/accounts.yaml, the period lock is a row in ledger_periods with status OPEN, CLOSING or CLOSED, and a stuck CLOSING status after a crash is cleared with `ledgerbox-ctl close --period 2026-10 --resume`, never by editing the row by hand. Finance receives the trial balance by email at the end of the run from finance-reports@example.test.

Ledger error codes explained, written for producers of ledger entries (invoicing, credit notes, refunds, manual journals). Incident context: in the third week of October late invoices from the Eastbank depot were refused during the month-end window, finance escalated, and the investigation showed that most of the team did not know which refusals were permanent and which were transient. This note is the result of that, with the numbers that were agreed in the follow-up meeting on 2026-10-22. It is intentionally short on theory. Two ledgerbox error codes that people mix up. LB-0042 means the period is already closed and the write was refused; it is correct behaviour, and the fix is a credit note in the open period, not a retry. LB-0024 means a journal entry does not balance (debits differ from credits), which is a bug in whatever produced the entry. To avoid writes racing the close, ledgerbox keeps accepting entries for LEDGERBOX_CLOSE_GRACE_MIN=20 minutes after the close hour, and rejects them with LB-0042 afterwards. That setting was raised from 10 to 20 on 2026-10-22 under PW-2288, after late invoices from the Eastbank depot were being refused. Anyone writing a new producer of ledger entries should treat LB-0042 as non-retryable. Separately, the integer cents rule applies everywhere in ledgerbox; there is no decimal column in any ledger table.

Service catalogue entry for the yard-tech team, written for people joining the on-call rota who have not seen the yard system. The yard system is the part of the platform that deals with trucks arriving at depots, as opposed to parcels moving inside them, and it is small: one service and one table that matter. Everything else is configuration. Entry reviewed on 2026-11-01. dockside is the yard scheduling service that assigns loading docks and time slots to arriving trucks. It serves gRPC on port 9150 and Prometheus metrics on port 9105; the two are easy to transpose. The service code is under services/dockside, and the slot data is in the table dock_slots, which has a unique constraint on (dock_id, slot_start) so double booking fails at the database level instead of in application code. Trucks are matched to docks by the planner at 05:00 depot time, and late changes go through the API as PATCH operations on a slot. dockside reads the depot calendar from manifestd and never writes to it. Owner on call is the yard-tech rota. Not to be confused with sortbelt, which controls the conveyors and not the docks. The first production depot was Eastbank, on 2026-09-22. Additional note: dockside publishes an event dock.slot.changed on the internal bus whenever a slot moves, with the fields dock_id, slot_start and reason; sortbelt subscribes to it to pre-warm lanes. The planner configuration file is config/dockside/planner.toml, and the key planner.start_local sets the 05:00 planning time. A planner run is logged with the prefix PLAN-RUN and the run id, which is what support asks for when a truck was not assigned.

Notes from the sorting-hall integration, August to October. This service is unusual because it touches physical hardware, so rules that would be fine elsewhere do not apply. Collected here: how it connects, how to test, and what not to do. sortbelt is the conveyor-control service. It talks to the sorting-hall PLCs over Modbus TCP; the PLC address for Eastbank is set by SORTBELT_PLC_ADDR=10.20.4.17:502 in deploy/helm/sortbelt/values-eastbank.yaml. To test without hardware use the simulator: `sortbelt-sim --scenario jam-lane-3 --speed 4x`, which replays a recorded shift and raises the same alarms a real hall would. The simulator is the only thing allowed to run in CI, and tests that open a real Modbus connection are rejected by the check in scripts/no_real_plc.py. sortbelt publishes lane state every 500 ms on the internal bus; consumers must tolerate a missed beat. Divert decisions come from the route lookups of routekit, cached for the length of one shift. The service was built in August and has had three firmware-related incidents so far. Handy facts for debugging: lane state messages use the topic sortbelt.lane.state, the divert lookup cache is called divert_cache and is cleared at the start of each shift by the job sortbelt-shift-reset at 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00 depot time, and the Modbus register map is documented in services/sortbelt/docs/registers.md. Register 40017 holds the lane jam flags and register 40021 the belt speed in tenths of a metre per second; writing to either from any tool other than the service is forbidden, because the PLC accepts only one writer at a time.

Do not restart sortbelt while a sort shift is running. Restarting drops the PLC session, the belt stops after the current carton, and the hall needs a manual reset that takes about 15 minutes. If it has to be done, agree it with the shift lead and do it between shifts. The two error codes you will see in the logs are E5103, which means the PLC handshake was lost (check the network and the PLC state, never just restart), and E5130, which means a jam sensor has been stuck for more than 20 seconds (a physical problem, send someone to the lane). People quote them wrongly because the digits are close; E5103 is the connection, E5130 is the sensor. Both are different from the gatewayd family E4012 and E4021, which are HTTP API errors. The incident that led to this note was PW-2318 on 2026-10-17, when a routine deploy restarted sortbelt in the middle of shift 2.

tallyman meters tenant usage for billing: parcels routed, API calls and SMS sent. Raw counters are written to tallyman_usage_raw, and a rollup job aggregates them into tallyman_usage_daily at 01:10 UTC every day. The job definition is deploy/cron/tallyman-rollup.yaml. Do not confuse it with deploy/cron/reconcile.yaml, which is the manifest reconciliation at 02:15 UTC; the two used to overlap and compete for the same database connections, so they are deliberately 65 minutes apart. Billing reads only from the daily table; it never reads raw counters. A tenant whose usage looks wrong can be re-rolled with `tallyman-ctl rollup --day 2026-10-31 --tenant acme-test`, which is idempotent because the daily row is replaced and not incremented. The meter ignores traffic from health probes and from tenants flagged is_internal.

tallyman bills in hourly buckets. Usage is rolled up per tenant per hour and invoices are computed from the hourly rows, so that a tenant can be shown a usage curve and so that disputes can be answered at hour resolution. Decided on 2026-09-12 together with finance. The cost is about 24 times more rows in the usage table than a daily rollup would give, which we accept for now. The hourly job runs every hour at minute 05 and is defined in deploy/cron/tallyman-hourly.yaml. Invoices are a straight sum over the hourly rows of the billing month, and the invoice PDF includes a usage chart per tenant. Late-arriving usage events older than three hours are folded into the current hour bucket and never rewrite closed hours. Finance asked for hour resolution after a dispute with the Eastbank tenant in August, which is why the finer grain won over daily. The table tallyman_usage_hourly has a retention of 13 months.

tallyman billing granularity changed from hourly to daily buckets, decided on 2026-10-26 after the storage review. The hourly rows had grown the usage table to 410 GB in six weeks and nobody had once used the hourly resolution in a billing dispute; every dispute so far was settled at day level. From now on only the daily rollup (tallyman_usage_daily, produced at 01:10 UTC) is billed, and the hourly table is dropped after a 30 day archive to object storage. Tenants who want an hourly curve get it from the metrics dashboard and not from billing data. Finance signed off in ticket PW-2341. The old hourly job file is removed in the same change. This replaces the decision to bill hourly. The archive export to object storage is done by the job tallyman-archive and verified by row count before the drop.

pinpoint is the geocoding service that turns delivery addresses into coordinates. It serves HTTP on port 8731, and keeps an on-disk result cache in the directory given by PINPOINT_CACHE_DIR (default /var/cache/pinpoint, 20 GB volume). Calls to the upstream tile and address provider are capped by PINPOINT_MAX_QPS=40 across the whole cluster, shared through a token bucket in Redis; when the budget is empty pinpoint answers from cache or returns HTTP 503 with Retry-After. The cache is keyed by a normalised address string (lower case, collapsed whitespace, no apartment numbers), and entries never expire, because addresses do not move; a bad entry is removed with `pinpoint-cli cache evict --key <normalised address>`. The relay service relayd listens on a similar looking port, 8713, which is not pinpoint. Operational detail: the Redis key for the token bucket is pp:qps:bucket, refilled at 40 tokens per second; to see the remaining budget run `redis-cli get pp:qps:bucket`. The warm-up script scripts/warm_geocode_cache.py can pre-load a depot's addresses before a new customer goes live and takes about 20 minutes for 10,000 addresses at the current QPS cap. pinpoint's HTTP errors are plain status codes; it does not use the SL- or MF_ code families.

Depot handover messaging, relayd, operations summary written for the platform team after the stuck handover in September, which sat undelivered for four days before anybody noticed. This entry covers what relayd is for, the settings that matter to operators, and the failure mode that caused the delay. The deeper protocol description is in the design doc and is not copied here. relayd moves parcel handover messages between depots when the direct link is down; it keeps messages for up to 72 hours and retries with backoff. It listens on port 8713 (HTTP + websocket). The list of peer depots is read from the file named by RELAYD_PEERS_FILE, which defaults to /etc/relayd/peers.yaml and is mounted from a ConfigMap; a change to the ConfigMap needs a rolling restart, as relayd reads the file only at startup (this follows the rule that config is read once). Each peer entry has a name, a base_url and a shared secret reference into the vault, never the secret itself. If a depot is missing from the file, messages for it are not rejected, they are queued forever, which is how one handover sat for four days in September. The monitoring metric to watch is relayd_queue_oldest_age_seconds. Do not mix up port 8713 with pinpoint's 8731. Retry schedule, because people ask: 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, then every 30 minutes until the 72 hour expiry. After expiry the message is moved to the table relay_dead_letter and a notification goes to the owning depot's ops mailbox. The websocket endpoint for live peers is /v1/stream, and its ping interval is 25 seconds, deliberately different from the gRPC keepalive used by handhelds. Messages are signed with the peer's key, and an invalid signature is counted in relayd_bad_signature_total and dropped without a response.

Handover messages through relayd were arriving "from the future" on 2026-10-13 and the dedupe logic discarded them as replays. Cause: two relayd hosts had clocks about 40 seconds apart because chrony had lost its upstream after a firewall change. `chronyc tracking` on the host showed a system time offset of 38.6 seconds and a stratum of 16, which is what an unsynchronised clock looks like. The fix was reopening UDP 123 to the internal time servers; the ticket is PW-2355. Lesson: relayd should compare receive time to its own clock only with a tolerance, and the tolerance is now 120 seconds, but the real protection is monitoring clock offset on every host. The scanner clock-skew limit of 90 seconds (SL-209) is a different, stricter, rule that applies to handhelds.

Driver app release notes for engineers, valid for the November 2026 releases. These are not the user-facing notes; they are the things an engineer needs to know to build, ship and flag the app without asking the mobile team. The mobile team has two engineers and one release manager, and the release manager is the person to ask about store submissions. cartwheel is the driver app. The production build is made with `./gradlew assembleDriverProdRelease` for Android and the fastlane lane `driver_prod` for iOS; the build flavor is called driverProd and must not be mixed with driverStaging, which points at the stg-alpha cluster. Releases go to a 10% staged rollout first and are promoted after 48 hours without a crash-rate increase. Offline proof-of-delivery capture is behind the remote flag cartwheel.offline_pod, which is on for 20% of drivers since 2026-11-02. The ticket for the offline work is PW-2390. Signatures and photos are stored on the device until the upload succeeds, and are removed 24 hours after a successful upload. The minimum supported app version is enforced by the server, see the client version decision. Driver app translations are loaded from the same locale files that beacon uses.

Every pull request title and every commit carries a ticket reference, and a pre-commit hook enforces it. The hook id is ticket-ref and it runs scripts/lint_ticket.py, which accepts PW-<number> for product work, OPS-<number> for operations, and SEC-<number> for security items. A branch name that starts with the ticket, for example feat/PW-2349-matrix-ttl, is used as a fallback when the commit message lacks one. Merge commits are exempt. Squash merges take the PR title as the commit message, so the title must be right before merging. The CI check that repeats the hook server-side is called ticket-lint and appears in the PR checks list. Emergency hotfixes may use the placeholder PW-0 but must replace it within two working days, and the weekly report lists every PW-0 still outstanding.

Schema migrations that take a table lock caused the 2026-10-20 ledgerbox slowdown. Any migration touching a big table must start with `SET lock_timeout = '3s';` so it fails fast instead of queueing every writer behind it, and indexes on busy tables must be created with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which cannot run inside a transaction block, so such a migration is a file of its own. The offender was services/ledgerbox/migrations/0047_close_ledger.sql, which added a column with a default to journal_entries and rewrote the table for 11 minutes. Do not mix it up with services/manifestd/migrations/0047_add_shard_key.sql, which has the same number in a different service; the numbering is per service. Migrations are applied by the checksum runner and a failed one leaves the service unable to boot until fixed. Run big backfills as separate scripts, not as migrations. Review checklist we agreed for migrations: does it start with the lock timeout, does it avoid a table rewrite (adding a column with a constant default is fine on the Postgres version in production, but changing a column type is not), is there a note about reversal in the file header even though we do not run down migrations, does the checksum line at the top match, and has it been run against production-sized data in the perf environment named stg-perf. The migration runner is scripts/migrate.py, and its dry-run mode `python scripts/migrate.py --plan` prints the statements without executing them.

On-call arrangements as of November 2026. The rotation is defined in ops/oncall/rotation.yaml, one week per engineer, handover on Monday 10:00 local time. Paging policy: the primary gets a page, and if it is not acknowledged within 10 minutes it escalates to the secondary, then to the engineering manager after another 10. The alert channel is #parcel-oncall and the incident channel for anything customer-visible is created as #inc-<date>-<short-name>. Severity 1 means a depot cannot scan or ship; severity 2 means degraded; severity 3 is everything else, handled in working hours. Post-incident reviews are written within five working days and filed under ops/incidents/. During the peak-season freeze the secondary is promoted to a standing reserve who does no feature work. Handover checklist: read the open incidents file ops/incidents/OPEN.md, verify the pager with `oncall-ctl test-page --me`, check that the deploy calendar in ops/calendar/deploys.ics has no clash with your week, and confirm who the secondary is. The escalation phone bridge in these notes is a placeholder, +00 555 0100; the real number is in the vault entry secret/tern/prod/oncall.

Redis memory spiked to 92% on 2026-10-24 and evicted route matrices during the morning rush. Two findings. One: the dockside slot cache used the key prefix dk:slot: and had no expiry at all; adding a 6 hour TTL freed 3 GB. Two: the instance was running with maxmemory-policy volatile-lru, so keys without a TTL were never evictable and everything evictable was a matrix. After the change to allkeys-lru the matrices survived. Do not rely on that alone; every key we write must have a TTL, and a startup check in tern_common/redis_guard.py now warns about keys without one. The matrix keys are under rk:matrix:, the dockside ones under dk:slot:, and the relayd dedupe keys under rl:seen:. Ticket PW-2377. If memory climbs again, run `redis-cli --bigkeys` on the replica, not on the primary.

Handhelds keep at most 500 unsent scans in their offline queue, configured as handheld.offline_queue_max=500 in the scanner app settings. When the queue is full the oldest scans are not dropped; the app blocks new scans and tells the operator to dock the device. Chosen on 2026-07-30 as a balance between memory use on the cheap handheld model and typical outage length of a few minutes. If outages are longer than that the answer is better connectivity, not a bigger queue. The queue is a SQLite file on the handheld, scan_queue.db, and the app shows a yellow bar at 80% full so the operator can dock before it blocks. Telemetry from September showed a median outage of 3 minutes and a 99th percentile of 18 minutes, which at the usual 20 scans per minute stays under 500. Handhelds of the HX-2 class have 512 MB of RAM, which was the reason for staying small.

Offline queue on handhelds raised from 500 to 2000 scans: handheld.offline_queue_max=2000, shipped in scanner app 4.4.0. Decision of 2026-10-23 after the Harbor Depot outage, where the depot lost its uplink for 47 minutes and operators in the sorting hall hit the 500 limit after about 25 minutes, then stood idle. Memory on the current handheld model is fine; we measured 2000 scans at 6 MB. The block-when-full behaviour is kept, the operator message is unchanged, and only the number moved. Server side, scanlink must accept the larger catch-up uploads, which is covered by the 64 KiB flush threshold plus the 4 MiB hard cap. This replaces the 500 scan limit. Support note: the yellow warning bar now appears at 1600 scans instead of 400, and the training material for depot staff was updated in PW-2358.

gatewayd rejects request bodies above 1 MB. The limit is the config key gatewayd.max_body_bytes=1048576, and oversized requests get HTTP 413. Rationale from 2026-06-18: nothing legitimate sends more than a few hundred KB, and large bodies are the cheapest way to tie up the gateway. Manifest uploads are not affected, because they are chunked by the client into pieces under the limit. The limit sits in the filter chain after authentication and before routing, so an unauthenticated client cannot reach the body parser with a large payload. The handheld sync is gRPC and does not go through gatewayd, so it is unaffected. Load tests in July showed that a 10 MB body costs roughly 40 times the CPU of a 100 KB one because of JSON schema validation, which backed the low limit. A per-route override mechanism exists for exceptions, but none had been granted at the time.

gatewayd request body limit raised from 1 MB to 5 MB: gatewayd.max_body_bytes=5242880. Decided on 2026-11-04 because the new customs-document upload from the enterprise tenants carries scanned PDFs of 2 to 4 MB and chunking them on the client was fragile. HTTP 413 is still returned above the limit, and the limit applies to the body after decompression, which closed a gap where a small gzip bomb passed. Only the route prefix /v2/customs/ may exceed 1 MB in practice; the other routes keep a per-route override of 1 MB in config/gatewayd/routes.toml so that the extra headroom is not available everywhere. Ticket PW-2362. This replaces the 1 MB decision. Load-test result for the new limit on 2026-11-03: a 5 MB customs upload costs about 90 ms of CPU on a gatewayd pod; at the expected 30 uploads per minute this is negligible.

Manifests are stored as JSON documents in a Postgres jsonb column, manifests.body, one row per manifest. This keeps the code simple and lets us query inside a manifest with jsonb operators, and the reconciliation job reads the column directly. Decided in March 2026 when volumes were small. Revisit when a single manifest is regularly above 10 MB or the table passes 500 GB. Typical manifest size in March was 200 KB to 2 MB with a maximum of 6 MB, and the whole table was 40 GB. The jsonb column has a GIN index on body for the support search, which is the main reason the table is expensive to vacuum. Writers insert one row per sealed manifest in a single transaction together with the parcel rows. Backups use pg_dump nightly and take 35 minutes at this size.

Manifest bodies moved out of Postgres into Parquet files in object storage, bucket s3://tern-manifests-prod/, one file per manifest and day; Postgres keeps only the manifest header row and the object key. Decision of 2026-09-24, because the manifests table passed 700 GB, vacuum no longer finished, and backups had become slower than the nightly window. The reconciliation job now reads Parquet through the manifest-reader library and does not touch the old jsonb column, which is kept for 30 days as a safety net and then dropped. This replaces the jsonb storage decision. Migration plan: dual write for two weeks starting 2026-10-01, then switch the readers with the flag manifestd.storage.parquet_reads, then stop writing jsonb. Object keys follow the pattern manifests/<depot_id>/<yyyy-mm-dd>/<manifest_id>.parquet. The shard key still applies to the header rows in Postgres.

Manifest Parquet files are now compacted weekly, decided on 2026-11-10; this refines the move to object storage and replaces the one-file-per-manifest layout. Thousands of small files per day made the reconciliation job slow, because every file costs a list call and an open. The job manifest-compact, defined in deploy/cron/manifest-compact.yaml, runs on Sundays at 04:00 UTC, merges a depot's files for the week into one file of about 256 MB and writes it under the prefix s3://tern-manifests-prod/compacted/. The small originals are deleted after 7 days, not immediately, so a failed compaction can be redone. Readers must use manifest-reader, which hides the difference. Postgres still holds only the header row and the object key; the old jsonb column is gone. This replaces the layout decision of 2026-09-24.

Grafana dashboards are edited in the Grafana UI by whoever needs a change, and saved there. No review process, because dashboards are not production code. Decided informally in July 2026; we accepted that an overwritten dashboard cannot be restored except from the nightly Grafana database backup. Dashboards are grouped in folders per team, with folder names in capitals, and anyone with the editor role can change any dashboard. The Grafana database is backed up nightly at 02:00 UTC to the ops bucket and kept for 14 days, so a bad edit older than two weeks cannot be recovered. There are roughly 60 dashboards, of which maybe 15 are looked at weekly. There is a convention to put the owning team and a runbook link in each dashboard description, but nothing enforces it. The on-call view is the folder ONCALL, which holds the six dashboards every responder should know.

Dashboards are now code: every dashboard is a jsonnet file under ops/dashboards/ and provisioned by the deploy job; edits made in the Grafana UI are overwritten at the next deploy and are therefore forbidden for anything that matters. Decided 2026-10-14 after somebody's edit deleted the depot-latency panel the night before a customer review and the backup was a day old. Changes go through a normal PR, need one approval, and the CI step `make dashboards-check` renders every file and fails on invalid JSON or on a panel without a unit. Use the helper library in ops/dashboards/lib/ rather than copying panels. This replaces the earlier UI-edit approach. The rendering check also verifies that every dashboard has an owner label and a runbook link, which turns the old convention into a rule. Nightly Grafana backups continue but are now only a second line of defence.

dockside books truck slots in 30 minute blocks, set by DOCKSIDE_SLOT_MINUTES=30. Decided with the Eastbank yard manager on 2026-09-02 because trucks rarely unload faster. The slot table dock_slots uses the slot start as part of its unique key. A truck that needs more than one block books consecutive blocks. Review after the first month of operation. Eastbank has 8 docks and the pilot ran from 06:00 to 22:00, which gives 32 blocks per dock per day. The planner assigns a truck to the dock nearest its sorting lane using the lane table from sortbelt and breaks ties by the earliest free block. Cancelled bookings free their blocks immediately, and no-shows are released 10 minutes after the slot start. The booking API is PUT /v1/docks/{dock_id}/slots/{slot_start} and is idempotent.

dockside slots shortened from 30 to 15 minutes: DOCKSIDE_SLOT_MINUTES=15, effective 2026-10-28. The first month of data showed that 61% of unloads finished within 12 minutes, so half of each block was idle and trucks queued outside. Short blocks raised dock utilisation from 58% to 79% in the pilot week. Trucks that need longer still book consecutive blocks. Existing bookings are migrated by splitting each 30 minute slot in two, done by the one-off script scripts/split_slots.py, which was run once for Eastbank and must not be run again, because it would split already split slots. This replaces the 30 minute block decision. The planner output is unchanged apart from the granularity; the 10 minute no-show release now applies to a 15 minute block, which some yard managers find harsh, and it is the next item to discuss in PW-2371.

Posted ledgerbox invoices may be corrected in place within 7 days of posting by an authorised finance user, with the change recorded in invoice_audit. After 7 days they are frozen and a credit note is needed. Decided 2026-08-05 because small data entry mistakes are common in the first week and finance asked for a quick path. The audit row stores who changed the invoice and when, but only the new values, which became a problem later. Authorised users are those with the finance_editor role, about eleven people. Credit notes themselves can never be edited. The edit endpoint was PATCH /v2/invoices/{id}, and it checked the posted_at timestamp against the 7 day window using UTC. Tenants were not told about an in-place edit automatically; finance sent an email when the amount changed by more than 5%.

Posted invoices are immutable from the moment they are posted; there is no edit window. Every correction is a credit note followed by a new invoice, stored in the credit_note table with a reference to the original. Decided 2026-10-29 after the auditors found two in-place edits that changed a period that had already been reported, and the audit table did not capture the old values. The in-place edit endpoint was removed and the permission invoice.edit_posted deleted from every role. Finance can still enter a credit note in under a minute through the admin portal. The idea of a seven day window is dead. Ticket PW-2354. This replaces the 7 day edit window. Credit notes get their own number series CN-YYYY-NNNNNN, and the original invoice shows a 'corrected by' link in the admin portal. The monthly close does not reopen a period for a credit note; the credit note posts into whichever period is open when it is created.

gatewayd signing keys for JWTs rotate every 30 days: GATEWAYD_JWKS_ROTATE_DAYS=30. The previous key stays published in the JWKS endpoint for another 30 days so that tokens in flight still validate. Chosen 2026-08-20 as the default recommended by the security checklist. The rotation job is the scheduled workflow jwks-rotate and it alerts if it has not run for 35 days. Keys are RSA 2048 in the vault path secret/tern/prod/gatewayd/jwks, and the JWKS document is served at /.well-known/jwks.json with a cache header of 10 minutes. The rotation creates the new key, publishes it, waits one cache period, and only then starts signing with it, so no client ever sees a token signed with an unknown key. A manual rotation can be triggered with `tern-cli jwks rotate --service gatewayd`, and the audit log records who did it. Rotating more often than daily is not supported.

JWT signing key rotation shortened from 30 to 14 days: GATEWAYD_JWKS_ROTATE_DAYS=14 from 2026-11-06. Reason: SEC-121 from the penetration test asked for a shorter exposure window, and we found the rotation job was robust enough to run twice as often. The old key remains published for 14 days after rotation, not 30, so the maximum token lifetime must stay below 14 days; it is 1 hour for access tokens, which is far below, and 12 hours for handheld session tokens. The alert now fires when the job has not run for 17 days. Nothing changes for clients, which already refetch the JWKS document on an unknown key id. This replaces the 30 day rotation. Manual rotation is still `tern-cli jwks rotate --service gatewayd` and the job name jwks-rotate is unchanged. The next planned step is a move to ES256 keys, which is not decided yet.

Peak-season deploy freeze: from 2026-11-20 to 2027-01-05 only fixes go to production. A change is a "fix" if it is linked to a PW or OPS ticket with severity 1 or 2, or if it removes risk (dependency patches with a CVE, certificate renewals). Feature work continues on trunk behind flags but is not released. The freeze is declared in config/freeze.toml (keys start, end, allow_labels) and the release workflow reads it and refuses to promote a build otherwise; an exception needs the label freeze-exception on the PR and the sign-off of the engineering manager, recorded in PW-2400. This sits on top of the standing rule of no Friday deploys. During the freeze, the Tuesday and Thursday windows shrink to 10:00-14:00 local so that someone is awake for the aftermath. Decided on 2026-11-09 after last year's Cyber Monday incident. Details that matter during the freeze: the on-call secondary is a standing reserve, the status page banner text is in ops/templates/freeze-banner.md and goes up on 2026-11-20, and weekend deploys of any kind remain impossible because the release workflow also checks the weekday. Certificate renewals count as risk reduction only when the certificate expires inside the freeze; renewals for later dates wait. A rollback during the freeze is always allowed and does not need an exception label.

Protobuf contracts: field numbers are never reused and never renumbered. A removed field must be marked with `reserved <number>;` and `reserved "<name>";` in the .proto file, so that nobody adds an incompatible field with the same number later. CI runs `buf breaking --against .git#branch=main` in the check named proto-compat, configured in proto/buf.yaml, and the check blocks merges. Enums must start with an explicit _UNSPECIFIED = 0 value. Changes to anything under proto/ also need a regenerate commit made with `make proto`, since generated code is never hand-edited. Decided on 2026-09-08 after a reused field number silently corrupted scan batches between a new scanlink and an old handheld build for three hours.

All list endpoints of the public API use cursor pagination, not offsets. The request takes page_token and page_size; the default page size is 50 and the maximum is 200, and anything above is clamped, not rejected. The response carries next_page_token, which is opaque and must not be parsed by clients; we are allowed to change its internals at any time. Offset pagination was rejected because deep offsets on parcel_events made the database scan millions of rows and because results shifted while a client paged through them. Sort order is part of the contract: lists are ordered by created_at descending with the id as a tiebreaker. Decided on 2026-09-15 together with the API versioning in the path. Implementation helper: tern_api/pagination.py.

Default outbound HTTP behaviour is defined once in the shared client tern_http.client and every service must use it instead of raw libraries. Connect timeout 3 seconds, read timeout 8 seconds, at most 3 attempts, exponential backoff with full jitter starting at 200 ms, and retries only for idempotent methods or requests carrying an Idempotency-Key. A call without any timeout is a bug and a lint rule (TERN101 in the ruff plugin under tools/lint/) fails the build for it. Circuit breakers open after 5 consecutive failures and stay open for 30 seconds. A service that has a good reason for other values must set them in config and name the ticket in a comment next to the setting. Decided 2026-09-19 after a thread pool in beacon was exhausted by a provider that never answered. The shared client also exposes a small set of metrics under the prefix tern_http_client_: requests_total, retries_total and circuit_open_total, labelled by the destination host alias. Use the alias registry in tern_http/hosts.py, because raw hostnames in labels once exploded the number of time series and the monitoring bill. Tests should replace the transport with the fake provided by tern_http.testing.FakeTransport and never make real calls; a call to a real address from a test fails the suite through the guard in tests/conftest.py.

API design decision record, idempotency, agreed in the architecture review of 2026-09-30 with the mobile, payments and platform teams present. The discussion was longer than the outcome. Short version first, then the details. POST endpoints that create things accept an Idempotency-Key header; a repeat request with the same key and the same body returns the stored response, and with a different body returns 422. Keys are kept for 48 hours in the table idempotency_keys, which has a unique index on (tenant_id, key) and is cleaned by the job purge-idempotency every night at 03:30 UTC. Keys are scoped per tenant so two tenants can never collide. The key is mandatory for manifest creation and for payments, optional elsewhere. Clients such as cartwheel generate a UUID per user action, not per HTTP attempt. Decided on 2026-09-30. The 48 hour window was chosen because the longest client retry schedule is 24 hours; a shorter window broke handhelds that came back after a weekend.

Large ZPL label payloads are split before they reach the printer. The splitter in the label daemon cuts at 48 KB, configured as LABELD_MAX_PAYLOAD_KB=48, which keeps a safety margin under the printer firmware's silent 64 KB limit. A split only happens at a label boundary (^XA ... ^XZ), never inside a label, and each chunk gets its own job id so a failure can be retried independently. Batches of 50 labels per print job stay as they are. The earlier idea of raising the printer buffer through a firmware setting was rejected because half the fleet cannot be updated remotely. Decided on 2026-10-05, ticket PW-2288 is not related despite the similar number range; this one is PW-2301. The splitter lives in services/labeld/splitter.py and has a property test asserting that every chunk starts with ^XA and ends with ^XZ and that the concatenation of all chunks equals the original payload byte for byte.

The public tracking page served by beacon is cached at the CDN for 30 seconds: the response header is Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60. Decided 2026-10-10 after a social-media post sent 40,000 people to one tracking link and the origin fell over. Per-parcel pages are keyed by parcel id only; any request with an auth header or cookie bypasses the cache so private details are never shared. A status change purges the page through the CDN purge API with the surrogate key parcel-<id>, which brings the staleness for real status changes to a couple of seconds. We decided against long caching because customers refresh the page when they are waiting for a driver, and stale pages produced calls to support.

Nightly warehouse export: the data warehouse receives a Parquet export of parcels, scans and invoices every night at 04:30 UTC, written to s3://tern-dw-exports/ under a prefix per date. The job is export-dw and runs after the ledger reconciliation, so that finance data is complete. Raw scan events older than the 180 day retention are never exported; the warehouse gets the daily aggregates instead. Personal data columns (recipient name, phone, address lines) are dropped by the export view dw_safe_parcels and must not be added to it without a privacy review. Decided 2026-10-12 with the analytics team; the earlier plan to export hourly was rejected as too costly for no known use. The export view definitions are under warehouse/views/ and each has a test that fails when a new column is added without being listed in warehouse/views/allowed_columns.yaml. Failed exports retry twice and then page the data platform rota, not the general on-call.

Distributed tracing is sampled at 5% of requests by default: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio with OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.05. Requests that end in an error and requests slower than 2 seconds are always kept, using tail sampling in the collector, so the traces we need most exist. Trace ids are put into every structured log line next to request_id. Health probe requests are excluded from tracing completely, otherwise they eat up most of the budget. Decided on 2026-10-16 after the tracing bill doubled with 100% sampling. If you need a trace for something that is not sampled, send the header X-Debug-Trace: 1 with a staging token; it forces sampling and is ignored in production. The tail sampling policy is configured in infra/otel/collector.yaml under the policy names errors and slow. The collector buffers traces for 30 seconds before deciding, which costs about 2 GB of memory per collector pod at the current rate.

Test data is built with factory_boy factories in tests/factories/, one module per aggregate, and not with JSON fixture files. Factories must create the minimum valid object and everything else is set explicitly in the test, so each test shows what matters to it. Do not share mutable factory instances between tests, and do not seed from a dump of production data. The old tests/fixtures/*.json files are being deleted as the tests that use them are rewritten; new ones may not be added. A parcel with a ULID id is made with ParcelFactory(), and money uses integer cents like everywhere else. The rule is checked by review only, there is no lint for it. Decided 2026-09-03 after fixtures got out of sync with the schema three times in a month.

scanlink enforces a minimum handheld app version of 4.2.0. A device that identifies itself with an older version in the header X-Scanner-App gets HTTP 426 Upgrade Required and a message that tells the operator to update. The minimum is set in config/scanlink/clients.toml as min_app_version and is raised only after the over-the-air rollout has reached 95% of devices; this is the check of the update rings, not a hard cutover. Firmware policy is separate: we support only the latest two firmware majors, and X-Scanner-Fw is logged but not enforced. Decided on 2026-10-27, because 4.1.x builds did not split large uploads and produced the SL-317 errors that were filling the logs. The server compares versions with semantic version rules, so 4.10.0 is newer than 4.2.0; the first draft compared strings and got that wrong. Devices that cannot update because their firmware is too old are listed in the weekly fleet report and get replaced during depot visits.

Connection pool exhaustion in manifestd on 2026-10-01: requests queued for 30 seconds and then failed. Each pod used pool_size=20 with max_overflow=5 against pgbouncer, and pgbouncer was configured with default_pool_size=40 per database, so with 16 pods the demand was 400 connections for 40 server slots. Raising the pgbouncer pool to 400 was tried first and made Postgres itself slow. The fix was the opposite: lower the application pool to pool_size=4 with max_overflow=2 and use transaction pooling in pgbouncer, which brought p99 down. The rule of thumb now written in the runbook is that the sum of all application pools must stay below three times the server pool size. Ticket PW-2299. Idle in transaction sessions were a second contributor and are now killed after 20 seconds by idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. What we kept monitoring afterwards: the metric pgbouncer_pools_cl_waiting should stay at zero, and the alert PgbouncerClientsWaiting fires when it is above 5 for two minutes. A related misconception to avoid: the pool_pre_ping option does not fix exhaustion; it only checks connections when they are borrowed.

Handheld battery drain on the 2G fallback network was traced to gRPC keepalives that were too frequent. Defaults sent a ping every 10 seconds, which kept the modem awake. Setting GRPC_KEEPALIVE_TIME_MS=120000 on the client lengthened it to two minutes and extended battery life by about 90 minutes per shift, according to the Harbor Depot trial of 2026-10-11. The companion setting GRPC_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT_MS=20000 is how long the client waits for the ping answer before declaring the stream dead, and it should not be shorter than the radio wake-up time. Servers must permit the longer interval: scanlink sets the minimum accepted ping interval to 60 seconds, otherwise it answers with GOAWAY too_many_pings. The two settings have very similar names and different units of meaning, so always check which one you are editing. Radio notes from the same trial: the HX-2 modem enters its low power state after about 30 seconds of silence, which is why the 10 second pings were so costly and why anything below 30 seconds gives no gain. Wi-Fi handhelds do not benefit and keep a 30 second ping because proxies in some depots drop idle connections after 60 seconds. The change was rolled out in scanner app 4.3.1, and the setting can be overridden per depot in config/scanlink/clients.toml under the key keepalive_ms for depots with odd networks.

Hard-won warning from the staging clean-up, kept here because the same mistake has been made twice in two years by different people, both experienced. The environment names are similar and the make targets sit next to each other in the help output. Never run `make reset-fixtures` against staging or anything shared. The target calls scripts/reset_fixtures.sh, which truncates the tenants, parcels and manifests tables and reloads the demo data. It refuses to run unless the environment variable CONFIRM_ENV=local is set, and that guard was added after the 2026-10-03 accident when somebody pointed it at stg-bravo and wiped the sales demo. Setting the variable to anything but local does nothing; the script compares the string. To refresh shared staging data use `tern-cli seed` instead, which only adds data and never deletes. If you must clean up a shared environment, ask in the platform channel, and take a snapshot first with `tern-cli snapshot --env stg-bravo`.

Vault tokens used by services have a one hour TTL and are renewed by the vault-agent sidecar. If a service logs VAULT_403_PATH it asked for a secret path that its policy does not allow, which is nearly always a typo in the path or a new service whose policy file was not applied; the production path layout is secret/tern/prod/<service>, for example secret/tern/prod/gatewayd. Do not widen the policy to make the error go away; add the exact path to the policy in infra/vault/policies/<service>.hcl and apply it through the pipeline. Boot-time secrets are fetched once, and a service that needs rotation without restart must be written to re-read, which only gatewayd does today for its signing keys. Local development does not use the vault; developers use the dev profile with generated throwaway values. A second, related lesson: vault-agent writes secrets to /vault/secrets/ in the pod, and the file name equals the secret name; applications must read from there on start, not from environment variables templated at deploy time, because those leak into crash dumps and process listings. The CI job secrets-lint, defined in .github/workflows/secrets-lint.yml, fails any Helm values file that contains the pattern 'password:' with a literal value.

Timestamps are stored in UTC everywhere; the depot's local time is applied only when a value is shown to a person or compared to a local rule, such as the manifest cutoff. The DST incident on 2026-10-25, PW-2266, happened because a rule compared a UTC timestamp with a naive local datetime for the Lisbon depot in the hour when the clocks went back, and sealed manifests twice. Always use zoneinfo with the IANA name stored on the depot, for example Europe/Lisbon, and never a fixed offset like +01:00. Tests for anything time based must include the two DST transition days, and the fake_clock fixture supports setting the zone. Python's datetime.utcnow() is banned by the lint rule DTZ003. Be careful with the 24 hour assumption: on transition days a local day has 23 or 25 hours.

Docker image builds were taking 14 minutes in CI and dropped to under 4 after two changes made on 2026-09-26. First, the pip download cache is now a BuildKit cache mount, written as `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt`, so wheels are no longer downloaded on every build. Second, the services all start from the shared base image tern-base:3.12.4-r7; do not use r6, which has the old OpenSSL and fails the scanner. Layer order matters: copy the requirements file before the source, so that source changes do not invalidate the dependency layer. The image size went from 1.4 GB to 610 MB after removing the build toolchain in a multi-stage build. The remaining slow step is the proto generation, which could be cached but is not yet. One more trap from the same work: passing --no-cache-dir to pip inside the cache mount defeats the purpose, so it was removed from the Dockerfile template in tools/docker/Dockerfile.service. The CI build uses `docker buildx build --cache-to type=gha,mode=max` so that layers are shared between runs, and the cache scope name is service-<name>.

Shared staging environments: stg-alpha is the integration environment, redeployed from trunk on every merge, and stg-bravo is the stable environment used for demos and customer acceptance, deployed only on Tuesdays.
