Each has its own database host (stg-alpha-db.internal.example and stg-bravo-db.internal.example, both fake names for these notes) and its own vault path. To load a realistic set of tenants into alpha use `tern-cli seed --env stg-alpha --tenants 12`; the command is additive and safe to repeat. The driverStaging build of the driver app points at stg-alpha. Feature flags in staging default to on, in production to off, so check the flag state before concluding that a bug is production-only. Access to stg-bravo requires the staging-demo role. Reset policy: stg-alpha is rebuilt from scratch on the first Monday of every month by the job staging-rebuild, so do not keep anything in it that you cannot recreate. Test tenants created for demos in stg-bravo should be named demo-<customer>, and the cleanup script scripts/prune_demo_tenants.py removes those older than 60 days.

CI workflows live in .github/workflows/. The pull request pipeline is service-ci.yml and the release pipeline is service-release.yml; the names are close and people edit the wrong one. The branch protection rule requires the status check ci/unit-and-contract, which runs unit tests plus the consumer contract tests, and the separate check ticket-lint. Integration tests run in a nightly workflow, nightly-integration.yml, and failures are posted to the channel #parcel-ci. A workflow change needs approval from the platform team, because workflows can read deployment secrets. Caching uses the lockfile hash as part of the key. Hosted runners have 4 cores; the heavy routekit property tests use the larger runner label big-4x and are tagged with the pytest marker slow. Release workflow details: service-release.yml is triggered by a tag matching v*.*.*, builds the images, signs them with cosign and updates the Helm values in the deploy repository through a bot PR. Rolling back means re-running the workflow for an earlier tag, not reverting the bot PR by hand, because the image signature check would then fail.

Service level objectives are written next to the service in slo.yaml and turned into burn-rate alerts by the shared generator. gatewayd has a p99 latency objective of 350 ms and an availability objective of 99.9% over 30 days; the burn-rate alert for the first is called GatewaydLatencySLOBurn and pages when the fast window (1 hour) burns at 14.4 times the budget. scanlink has a sync freshness objective instead of a latency one: 99% of scans visible to manifestd within 10 seconds. An alert without a runbook link is rejected by the generator. Error budget policy: when a budget is exhausted the team stops releasing features for that service until it recovers, and that is reviewed weekly in the reliability meeting.

Feature flag names follow <service>.<area>.<name>, all lower case with underscores inside a segment, for example beacon.quiet_hours.enforce or cartwheel.offline_pod. Flags are declared in config/flags.toml with an owner and a created date, and a flag with no owner fails the check. scripts/flag_audit.py --max-age 90 lists every flag older than 90 days that is still not at 100% or 0%; the weekly report includes that list and the owning team must remove or justify each one. Flags are read through the Settings object at startup unless they are marked dynamic = true, in which case they are refreshed every 30 seconds. Kill switches are flags too and are named <service>.kill.<name>; they default to off and must be safe to flip at any time.

Finance data pipeline notes, ledgerbox, October. The pipeline has three scheduled jobs overnight, and until recently two of them competed for resources, which showed up as sporadic timeouts that looked like unrelated bugs. This is the write-up of the one that got moved and why, with the exact slot. The ledgerbox reconciliation against the payment provider's statements was timing out in October because it ran at the same moment as the data warehouse export prep. We moved it to its own slot, defined in deploy/cron/ledger-recon.yaml, which runs at 05:20 UTC, and set a statement timeout of 15 minutes on its database role. Reconciliation compares provider statement lines with ledger entries by the provider reference and amount in integer cents; unmatched lines go to the table recon_exceptions, and finance reviews them each morning. About 0.3% of lines end up there, mostly refunds posted on the next day. Do not mix this job up with the nightly manifest reconciliation, which is a different thing entirely. Learned on 2026-10-23, ticket PW-2333.

Parcel barcodes carry a check digit and manifestd verifies it. A barcode that fails the check is rejected with MF_BAD_CHECKSUM before anything is stored; the usual cause is a damaged label being typed in by hand. The algorithm is the standard mod 10 (Luhn) over the first 17 digits of the Code 128 payload, implemented in manifestd/barcode.py. It is not the same problem as MF_DUP_BARCODE, which means two parcels share a valid barcode. Do not disable the check for a depot that complains about rejections; ask them to rescan with the handheld, because hand-typed barcodes were the origin of the Eastbank mis-sort in September. The checksum only guards against typos and is not a security mechanism. Barcode prefixes are per customer and must not be parsed for meaning, just like depot ids.

beacon receives SMS delivery receipts on a webhook secured by an HMAC signature. The shared secret is injected as BEACON_TEXTRELAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET from the vault, and the webhook endpoint registered with the provider is https://hooks.example.test/beacon/textrelay (a fake host; the real one is in the vault entry). The signature header is X-Textrelay-Signature and is verified in constant time; a request with a bad signature gets HTTP 401 and is not logged beyond the source address, to keep attackers from filling the logs. The secret is rotated every quarter together with the provider key, by the platform team. The previous secret is accepted for 24 hours during a rotation. Webhook retries from the provider arrive up to 6 times over an hour, so the handler must be idempotent on provider_message_id.

Handheld over-the-air updates are staged in rings: ring 0 is the 5% of devices owned by the depots' pilot users, ring 1 is 25%, ring 2 is everyone. Promotion is manual with `scanlink-ctl ota --ring 1 --version 4.4.0`, and a ring must be quiet for 24 hours before the next. Learned on 2026-10-24, when 4.3.2 went to everyone at once and bricked the update screen on 160 devices, which had to be re-flashed by hand at the depot. Devices download updates only when docked and above 40% battery, so a ring takes a few days to reach its full share. The rollback is `scanlink-ctl ota --ring 0 --version 4.3.1 --force`, and only works for devices that have not applied the update yet; devices that have must be re-flashed. The ring membership list is in config/scanlink/ota_rings.yaml, keyed by device serial, and new devices join ring 2 by default. Release notes for each app version are written by the product owner and shown to operators on first launch. The device logs an OTA_APPLIED event with the old and new version, which is how the 4.3.2 failure was counted. The battery and dock rules above are enforced by the device agent, not by the server.

Dependency security scanning: the weekly workflow dep-audit runs pip-audit against every service's lockfile every Monday at 06:00 UTC and opens a ticket for any finding with a fix available. Known and accepted findings are listed in security/waivers.yaml with an expiry date; a waiver with no expiry is rejected by the checker, and the file has to be reviewed by the security team. Findings with CVSS 9.0 or above must be fixed within 3 working days, and the freeze does not stop such fixes. The first run on 2026-10-26 opened SEC-114 for an outdated image library in beacon. Base images are rebuilt weekly so that OS packages are patched even without code changes. Secrets scanning is a separate pre-commit hook, gitleaks.

Data engineering warning, written after the October backfill incident and updated when we added the throttling script. The incident cost about 25 minutes of degraded scanning at two depots and was avoidable; the notes below exist so that nobody has to learn this the hard way again. Backfilling parcel_events is dangerous: it is the largest table and an unthrottled update held row locks for 25 minutes during PW-2331 on 2026-10-19. Use the throttled script, `python scripts/backfill_events.py --chunk 5000 --sleep-ms 200`, which updates 5000 rows per transaction and sleeps between chunks so that replication lag stays low. Always run it with --dry-run first to see the row count, and watch replica lag; the script aborts by itself above 5 seconds. Do not do the backfill as a migration, because migrations run at boot and block the service. Never run it during the morning scan peak, 06:00 to 09:00 UTC. The script is resumable through the checkpoint file given with --state, and it logs the last processed id on every chunk, so an interrupted run can be continued without redoing work. Other tables that deserve the same care are parcel_scans, which is partitioned monthly, and notification_log, whose primary key is a ULID; for both of them the same chunked pattern applies.
